# Concepts — Dawit Bekele

Three concepts, differing in form and object. None chosen yet.

---

## Concept A — The Runbook

**The question.** What makes a migration boring on the day?

**The form.** His own migration runbook, in his own stage names, from his resume: preflight, shadow, dual write, cutover, soak, decommission.

| Chapter | Role | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| (opening, before preflight) | The opening | His name, the question, a single closed container at rest in a yard |
| Preflight | Who / Where from | The three jobs and their years — library, Lumen Pay, Kestrel — as the checks you do before you touch anything |
| Shadow | How | The way he works: the runbook, the checklist, the rollback plan; the 2014 dropped table as the shadow experience behind all of it |
| Dual write | What | The Kestrel migration itself, the Postgres 11→15 upgrade, ferry and its cutover command, the SRE North talk |
| Cutover | What came of it | 99.98% availability of the order API over 26 months, two sub-ten-minute internal incidents, pages per week 85→22 (said as "we," the on-call team of nine) |
| Soak | Proof that held | The runbook, still used by 40 teams; ferry, still maintained since 2022 |
| Decommission | (the old, switched off) | The old data centres; his old 2019 site, retired |
| (close, after decommission) | The close | The answer to the question, and how to write to him |

**The object.** Shipping containers — plain, stackable, identical at rest, five to twelve of them. Not the SRE emblem (no server racks, no globe of pings): these come from the company he's spent six years moving onto the cloud, a freight company, and from his own line about the work — "while the trucks kept running."

**What it becomes.**
- *Preflight:* the containers line up in a column, each stencilled with a job and its years, oldest at the bottom.
- *Dual write:* two full stacks stand side by side, on-prem and cloud, and small crates cross from one to the other one at a time, 310 of them, while one container is relabelled 11 → 15.
- *Cutover:* the stacks snap into one, and the containers' faces turn into stencilled numbers — 99.98%, 85→22, 40 teams.

**The opening and the close.** It opens on one closed container, alone, in a yard, with his name and the question. It closes on the full set standing together, whole and still, with the answer and an address to write to.

**What it stands on.** The runbook's stage names (resume), the 310 services and 26 months (resume, LinkedIn), 99.98%/order API/two sub-ten-minute incidents (confirmed), 85→22 pages said as "we," team of nine, about a year (confirmed), 40 teams (confirmed), ferry since 2022 with his cutover command (confirmed), the 2014 dropped table (confirmed), the old site retiring (confirmed).

**What it needs from him.** Nothing further to confirm. No picture is needed — the object is built, not photographed. If he'd like his talk video or slides linked at the point ferry/the talk appear, that's a yes to get (they're already public, by his own word).

**Why it's his.** The chapters are the exact words of the runbook he wrote and still owns, and the object is built from the freight business he has spent four years moving onto the cloud — no colleague at another company has this runbook, under these names, moving this freight.

---

## Concept B — The Rollback

**The question.** What do you build so a mistake doesn't become permanent?

**The form.** The rollback plan, the document he named second among the three he works from: the trigger that says something is wrong, the point of no return, the steps back, the check that it's really back.

| Chapter | Role | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| Opening | Name, the question | — |
| 2014 | Where from | The dropped table, the library, the first outage |
| The trigger | How | What he watches for now — the runbook, the checklist, the SRE book and *Release It!* |
| The point of no return | What | The Postgres 11→15 upgrade, run with dual writes precisely so there was always a way back |
| Steps back | What came of it | The two sub-ten-minute incidents during the Kestrel migration, and how they were recovered, not just that they happened |
| Verified | Proof | 99.98% over 26 months; the runbook now used by 40 teams |
| Close | Answer, contact | — |

**The object.** Stacked database-table blocks, labelled by schema version, five to twelve of them, one of which can be drawn out and the stack still stands. Not a control panel or a dashboard — those read as the reliability-engineer emblem. These are tables, because a table is the thing he dropped in 2014 and the thing he upgraded four versions later.

**What it becomes.**
- *2014:* one block, alone, tips and empties — the table he dropped.
- *The point of no return:* the full stack relabels from 11 to 15, one block at a time, each still removable.
- *Steps back:* a block is pulled from the middle of the stack and the rest hold — twice, for the two incidents — before settling again.

**The opening and the close.** Opens on the one block tipping, 2014, before his name has even settled on screen. Closes on the full stack, labelled 15, standing, with the answer and his contact.

**What it stands on.** The 2014 story, the Postgres upgrade, the two incidents, 99.98%, the 40 teams, the two books (all confirmed).

**What it needs from him.** Nothing further — same as A, no picture required.

**Why it's his.** The table is literally the object of his first and worst mistake, and the thing he later upgraded without a maintenance window; no emblem does that, because no one else dropped that table.

---

## Concept C — The Handover

**The question.** What does the next person on call need to know?

**The form.** The shift handover — the form a reliability team actually passes along at the end of a rotation: what's open, what to watch, what happened, what's next.

| Chapter | Role | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| Opening | Name, the question | — |
| What's open | Where from | The three jobs, in order, as unfinished business carried from one shift to the next |
| What to watch | How | The runbook, the checklist, the rollback plan, the books he learned from |
| What happened | What | The Kestrel migration, the Postgres upgrade, ferry, the talk |
| The numbers | What came of it | 99.98%, 85→22 pages (as "we"), 40 teams |
| What's next | Close | The answer, and how to reach him |

**The object.** A set of handover cards — plain index-card shapes, five to twelve of them, each passed from one hand-shape to the next as the page scrolls, each card's face carrying one fact.

**What it becomes.**
- *What's open:* the cards lay out in a line, oldest job first, like a hand of cards dealt in order.
- *What happened:* one card turns into the migration's two stacks (a small echo of concept A, held on a card's face rather than as the whole object).
- *The numbers:* the cards flip to show their numbers at once, like a hand turned face-up.

**The opening and the close.** Opens on a single card, blank side up. Closes on the full hand, face up, with the answer and his contact.

**What it stands on.** Same facts as A and B, read through the on-call rotation rather than the migration itself.

**What it needs from him.** Nothing further.

**Why it's his.** It is built from the literal practice of a shift handover, which he runs as on-call lead — but of the three, this is the one that leans most on a generic card-flip, and it says the least that A and C don't already say better.

---

## Which I would choose

**Concept A, The Runbook.** It's the closest reading of his own words: the runbook's six stages are already named, in order, on his own resume, and he told us directly it's one of the three documents he works from. The object — shipping containers — comes from the one detail that is unmistakably his and not a reliability engineer's in general: four years spent moving a freight company's services, one at a time, onto the cloud, "while the trucks kept running." Concept B is a close second and holds the 2014 story with more weight; if he wants the dropped table to carry more of the page than one scene, B is the one to open with instead. Concept C is the weakest of the three — the handover is real, but the card object says less than A's containers or B's tables, and leans closer to a generic flip-card effect than either.

Form: his own runbook — preflight, shadow, dual write, cutover, soak, decommission.

Not built yet. This is the script.

## The beats

### Chapter 0 — Opening

| 0.1 | 1 | One container, alone, centred, closed | Blank — no stencil yet | A low, still camera; a cold empty yard | "Dawit Bekele." / "What makes a migration boring on the day?" |

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |

| 7.1 | 1 | The full set — opening container plus every stage's containers — stand together, whole, evenly lit | Each keeps the one stencil that matters most from its chapter | — | "What makes a migration boring on the day? Checking what's running before you touch it. Running it twice before you trust it. Always having a way back." |
| 7.2 | 1 | Same shot, still | — | Contact block appears over the scene | "Going independent in 2027. Looking for a company about to run a migration it's afraid of, or a conference that wants the talk. Write to him: [email]. CV. ferry. The talk. The slides." |

## Someone with thirty seconds

The opening screen (0.1) carries the name and the question. A fixed rail, visible from the first scroll onward, lists all seven chapters by name and jumps to any of them; one of its items is always "Close," which jumps straight to beat 7.2 — the answer and every way to reach him. Someone who reads only the opening and taps "Close" gets: his name, the one line of what he does (the question itself, plus the answer in 7.1), one proof (whichever number is already visible behind the contact block, e.g. "99.98%"), and the email/CV. That is the three-part minimum in under thirty seconds, no scrolling required.

## Without the scene

The text in every beat's caption is ordinary HTML laid over the 3D, never only inside it, so all of it is present in every row below regardless of what renders.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | The same beats and captions, in the same order. The live WebGL scene is replaced by the same arrangements pre-rendered as a short sequence of still frames (one per beat), advanced by scroll position rather than by a live camera — same stencils, same numbers, same order. Tap replaces hover for the container detail cards. The rail collapses to a single "chapters" button. |
| With reduced motion | Every beat still renders, but transitions between beats become instant cuts or simple fades — no camera movement, no crate-crossing animation, no tipping container. The counter in 3.2 appears already at its final value rather than climbing. All text, numbers and order are unchanged. |
| With no WebGL | The containers appear as flat, stencilled illustrations — the same look's ink and accent colour, drawn as simple shipping-container icons — one static image per beat, laid out in the chapters' order. Every caption, number, and link still appears, in the same order, beside its image. |
| With no JavaScript | A single plain HTML page: the chapters in order, each as a heading (its form name, e.g. "Preflight") followed by its captions as ordinary paragraphs, in beat order, with no images. All links — CV, ferry, the talk, the slides, email — work as plain anchors. Nothing about the story's order or wording changes; only the pieces are gone. |

## The look and the type

The object's material is painted steel, stencilled in yard paint — so the ground, ink and surface all come from a shipping yard, not from a generic "dark developer portfolio" palette. Three looks, built the same way, for Dawit to scroll through once there's something to scroll:

**1. Dockyard overcast.** Ground: cool slate grey. Ink: near-white. Accent: stencil orange (the colour freight stencilling actually uses). Surface: brushed, slightly weathered steel — visible weld lines, faint rust at the corners, nothing shiny. Reads as daylight, Rotterdam-grey, matter-of-fact.

**2. Night yard.** Ground: near-black navy. Ink: pale cyan-white. Accent: sodium-vapour amber, the colour of dock floodlights. Surface: dark painted steel, higher contrast, longer shadows. Reads as after-hours, the hour an on-call page actually comes in.

**3. Manifest paper.** Ground: warm off-white, close to kraft paper. Ink: dark ink-blue. Accent: stencil red. Surface: flatter, drawn rather than photoreal — closer to a technical illustration of a container than a render of one. Reads lighter and more approachable; the option if the other two feel too heavy for a site meant to invite a nervous client to write in.

Two typefaces: a plain humanist sans for all body text and captions, chosen for long reading comfort, not character; and a stencil face — the kind actually cut into shipping-container lettering — used only on the pieces themselves, for every stencilled word and number on a container's face. The two are never mixed within one block of text.

## Everything else the site needs

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | Build — one scroll, plus the fixed chapter rail described above | Me (follows from the concept) |

Here's the full plan, written to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

## The idea

Question: **What makes a migration boring on the day?**
Form: your own runbook — preflight, shadow, dual write, cutover, soak, decommission — the exact stages from your resume.
Object: plain stencilled shipping containers. Not a server rack, not a dashboard — containers, because you've spent four years moving a freight company's services while "the trucks kept running," in your own words.

## The scroll, top to bottom

- **Opening** — your name, the question, one closed container alone in an empty yard.
- **Preflight** (Who/Where from) — the container becomes three, stencilled with each job and its years: the library, Lumen Pay (shown only as "card payment systems," nothing more), Kestrel.
- **Shadow** (How) — faint mirror outlines beside the stack; one separate container tips and spills — the 2014 dropped table, the origin of why you care about rollbacks; the runbook, checklist and rollback plan appear as labels, then the two books.
- **Dual write** (What) — two stacks, on-prem and cloud, with crates crossing one at a time toward 310 as you scroll; one container relabels 11→15 (the Postgres upgrade); ferry and the talk appear as their own small containers, each linking out.
- **Cutover** (What came of it) — the stacks snap into one; faces flip to your real numbers: 99.98% (order API, 26 months, two sub-ten-minute internal incidents), 85→22 pages/week ("we," the team of nine), 40 teams on the runbook.
- **Soak** (proof that held) — the stack just sits still for a beat. Nothing moving is the point.
- **Decommission** — the old on-prem containers lift away and fade; your old 2019 site fades out too.
- **Close** — the full set stands whole; the answer to the question, then email, CV, ferry, the talk, the slides.

## Touch, phone, and the fallbacks

A fixed rail jumps to any chapter and always has a "Close" shortcut, so someone with thirty seconds gets your name, the question, one number, and how to reach you without scrolling at all. On a phone, the same beats play from pre-rendered stills advanced by scroll position, tap instead of hover. With reduced motion, beats cut instead of animate. With no WebGL, flat stencilled illustrations stand in, same order, same text. With no JavaScript, it's a plain HTML page — same chapters, same captions, same links, just no pieces.

## Look and type

Three options to pick from once there's something to scroll: **Dockyard overcast** (slate grey, near-white ink, stencil-orange accent, weathered steel), **Night yard** (near-black navy, amber floodlight accent, higher contrast), or **Manifest paper** (warm kraft tone, ink-blue, flatter illustrated containers — lighter and more approachable). Body text in a plain sans; anything stencilled on a container face uses an actual stencil typeface.

## Everything else, and what's still yours to call

Full checklist is in the storyboard's last table — retiring the old site, a 404 themed as an empty decommissioned container, no blog/chat/per-project pages for now. Four things are still open and need your word: whether a CV PDF exists to link or the site should be the CV, whether to add Dutch alongside English, which of the three looks feels most like you, and whether the site should carry analytics or log nothing at all.

Everything I decided without asking, and how to undo each, is in `docs/story/decided-for-you.md`.
